Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Daniel 5, drawn from the pages I was able to read.

---

## DANIEL 5 – VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — “Later, King Belshazzar held a great feast for a thousand of his nobles…”

**Historical background.** Belshazzar was not the immediate successor of Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar died after a 43-year reign; his son Evil-Merodach ruled two years before being assassinated; Neriglissar ruled four years; his child-son Laborosoarchod ruled nine months before being killed by conspirators. They appointed Nabonidus, whose eldest son Belshazzar served as co-regent while Nabonidus lived in retirement in Arabia (Tema). At the time of Daniel 5, Nabonidus had likely already been captured by the Medo-Persian army, leaving Belshazzar as the acting king in Babylon. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

Gill notes that Belshazzar’s name means “Bel’s treasurer” or “Bel protect the king,” and that this feast may have been an annual festival in honour of a Babylonian deity (the Sacaean feast), known for days of drinking and revelry. The size of the feast is not implausible — ancient historians record that Persian kings routinely dined with up to 15,000 guests, and Alexander the Great once entertained 10,000. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]; [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

**Spiritual significance.** Belshazzar was feasting while the Medo-Persian army surrounded the city. He felt secure because Babylon’s walls were massive (17 miles around, 22 feet thick, 90 feet high, with bronze gates and a moat system). The city had not fallen to an invader for 1,000 years. Guzik notes this “reminds us of the spirit of our present age” — escaping danger through the pursuit of pleasure. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Septuagint (LXX) offers a different opening: “Baltasar the king made a great feast on the day of the dedication of his palace, and invited from his lords two thousand men,” suggesting the feast may have been a palace dedication. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-5.html]

### v. 2 — “Under the influence of the wine, Belshazzar gave orders to bring in the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken…”

**“His father Nebuchadnezzar.”** Nebuchadnezzar was Belshazzar’s grandfather (or possibly a more remote ancestor), not his direct father. The term “father” was used in ancient Near Eastern languages for any male ancestor; there is no separate word for “grandfather” in Biblical Aramaic or Hebrew. Gill notes Belshazzar was the son of Evil-Merodach and grandson of Nebuchadnezzar. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]; [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

**Sacrilege.** Gill says the vessels had been stored in the temple of Bel (Daniel 1:2) and were now brought out. The Pulpit Commentary suggests Belshazzar’s act may have been a deliberate defiance of Jehovah of Israel — he may have suspected the Jews were in league with Cyrus and used the vessels to assert the superiority of Babylon’s gods. It adds that the presence of “wives” and “concubines” (absent from the LXX’s shorter version) heightens the degradation. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-5.html]

Guzik calls this “the sin of sacrilege, something few people are concerned with today,” and quotes John Trapp: “As if these dung-hill deities had mastered and spoiled the God of Israel… This was blasphemy in a high degree.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

### vv. 3–4 — “Thus they brought in the gold vessels… they drank wine… praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.”

Gill notes that only the “gold” vessels are mentioned as being brought, though the silver ones were certainly included — the gold ones are singled out because of their greater value. He adds that they drank “till they were drunk” and praised their gods by singing songs, drinking healths, and ascribing their victories over the nations to their idols, thus insulting the God of Israel. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the description of the gods as mere materials (gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, stone) “probably reflects the Hebrew perspective of the writer” — for Israelites these were no gods at all. Dr. Constable adds that Belshazzar may have been trying to strengthen nationalistic pride among the Babylonians as Cyrus’s army pressed in. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### v. 5 — “At that moment the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall, near the lampstand…”

**“In the same hour.”** Gill observes that the judgment came at the very moment the blasphemy was being committed — God’s timing was immediate and precise. Some rabbinic traditions (noted by Gill) speculated the hand was Gabriel’s, but Gill dismisses this as conjecture. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]

**The lampstand.** The Aramaic word *nebhrashta* later became equivalent to *menorah* in Talmudic times, leading some to believe the golden lampstand from the Jerusalem temple had also been brought to the hall. The Pulpit Commentary suggests that “opposite the lampstand” indicates the writing appeared where it was clearly visible by the light. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-5.html]

**Archaeological note.** Dr. Constable reports that in the ruins of Nebuchadnezzar’s palace, archaeologists have uncovered a large throne room 56 feet wide and 173 feet long — likely the scene of this banquet. Midway on the long wall opposite the entrance there was a niche with white plaster, exactly as Daniel describes, which would have made an excellent background for the writing. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### v. 6 — “his face grew pale and his thoughts so alarmed him that his hips gave way and his knees knocked together.”

Gill describes the physical effects vividly: Belshazzar’s “brightness” — his florid, joyful countenance — vanished into paleness. His “joints” or “girdles of his loins” were loosened — some commentators (Grotius, noted by Gill) suggest he lost control of his bladder. Gill adds: “his knees smote one against another; as is the case of persons in a great tremor, or under a panic.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]

Guzik notes: “Belshazzar was terrified. His carefree partying was so shallow that it turned from merry to terrified in a moment. This shows that his conscience was active beneath his energetic partying.” He quotes Trapp: “The writing on the wall he could neither read nor understand; but his conscience had written bitter things against him, which now being held to the fire of God’s wrath become legible.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

### v. 7 — “The king called out for the enchanters, astrologers, and diviners… third highest ruler…”

**The “third” ruler.** This is an important historical detail confirmed by archaeology. Belshazzar was himself the second ruler in the kingdom (under his father Nabonidus), so the highest position he could offer was third. Guzik notes this “detail archaeology has confirmed.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

**The reward.** Purple clothing signified royal authority. The gold chain had both symbolic and monetary value. The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Septuagint version has the wise men entering *before* the reward is announced, which “makes the succession of events more natural” — the king first calls them, they fail, and then he proclaims the reward. The LXX also omits any requirement to *read* the writing — only to interpret it. This may suggest the words were written in characters the wise men could not decipher. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-5.html]

### vv. 8–9 — “So all the king’s wise men came in, but they could not read the inscription or interpret it…”

**Why couldn’t they read it?** Several theories exist. Gill lists them: the words may have been written in Samaritan or Phoenician characters unfamiliar to Babylonians; they may have been written without vowel points; the letters may have been arranged vertically or backwards; or they may have been ligatured into a single string. But Gill concludes the true reason was divine — God blinded their minds so Daniel would be called. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]

Dr. Constable notes that the words were likely Aramaic, the common language. The difficulty was not in pronouncing them but in interpreting what they signified for Belshazzar. The words were weight-names (mina, shekel, half-shekels) — meaningless as a message without the context Daniel supplied by adding different vowels to the consonantal text. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### vv. 10–12 — “Hearing the outcry… the queen entered… ‘There is a man in your kingdom…’”

**Identity of the queen.** All the commentators agree she was the *queen mother*, not Belshazzar’s wife. His wives were already at the feast (vv. 2–3). She entered from outside. Gill identifies her as Nitocris, the widow of Evil-Merodach and daughter of Nebuchadnezzar; Josephus thought she was Nebuchadnezzar’s widow (Belshazzar’s grandmother). Constable says she was probably Belshazzar’s mother, a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar, and notes that queen mothers held considerable influence in ancient courts (cf. 1 Kings 15:13; 2 Kings 11:1–3). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]; [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

**Daniel’s absence.** The queen’s need to remind Belshazzar of Daniel indicates Daniel had not been called with the other wise men. Guzik suggests Daniel “was semi-retired, still holding a government office yet not a main figure in the administration.” Gill observes that Daniel had likely been removed from his offices after Nebuchadnezzar’s death; had he still held high office, the queen would have described him by his title. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]; [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/5.htm]

**“Spirit of the holy gods.”** The queen uses polytheistic language — “holy gods” rather than “the Holy God.” This suggests she was not a believer in Yahweh but had respect for Daniel’s gifts. Yet she refers to Daniel by his Hebrew name (not Belteshazzar), showing respect for his faith. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

### vv. 13–16 — “So Daniel was brought before the king… ‘Are you Daniel, one of the exiles…?’”

Belshazzar’s words reveal he does not know Daniel personally: “Are you that Daniel…?” He knows of Daniel only by reputation, and even condescendingly notes he is “one of the captives from Judah.” Guzik notes that Belshazzar “didn’t think to call for Daniel himself” and quotes Trapp: “This silly and shallow prince hath nothing to say but what was put into his mouth by his wiser grandmother.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

Dr. Constable points out the irony: a worshipper of the God Belshazzar had been dishonouring might now prove superior to all the Chaldean wise men. The king was desperate enough to honour a Jewish exile. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### v. 17 — “You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else…”

Daniel’s refusal of the gifts is significant. Guzik notes that Daniel had been troubled when he had to deliver bad news to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:19), but here he “was not impressed with this successor” and shows no anxiety. Constable adds that declining the gifts ensured Belshazzar understood the interpretation was not influenced by reward. Gill compares Daniel to Elisha refusing Naaman’s gifts (2 Kings 5:16). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]; [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### vv. 18–21 — “…the Most High God gave your father Nebuchadnezzar sovereignty…”

Daniel prefaces the interpretation with a sermon. He rehearses Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling — how God gave him greatness, but when his heart became arrogant, he was deposed, driven to live like a beast, until he acknowledged that “the Most High God rules over the kingdom of mankind.” Constable calls it “a powerful sermon” and notes that Daniel was reminding everyone in the hall of the lesson in humility from chapter 4. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### vv. 22–23 — “But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this…”

Daniel’s accusation is that Belshazzar *knew* what happened to Nebuchadnezzar yet refused to humble himself. Instead he exalted himself against “the Lord of heaven,” desecrated the temple vessels, praised lifeless idols, and failed to glorify “the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.”

Guzik stresses: “We are all responsible to honour God according to what revelation we have. Belshazzar should have known even more through God’s dealings with and through Daniel.” He adds that “the breath of the creature should praise the Creator, but Belshazzar blasphemed God with his breath.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

Constable notes that “one of the most amazing spectacles in this world is how little men really profit from the judgments of God.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### vv. 24–28 — “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN… God has numbered… weighed… divided…”

**The inscription.** The words are Aramaic names of weights: a *mina* (about 50 shekels), a *shekel*, and *half-shekels* (or “and half-shekels”). This is why the wise men could not interpret them — the list of weights made no sense as a message. Daniel supplied different vowels to the consonantal text, reading the words as passive participles: *MENE* = “numbered,” *TEKEL* = “weighed,” *PERES* (singular of *PARSIN*) = “divided.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

**Why “MENE” twice?** Constable explains that the repetition stresses certainty, just as Joseph told Pharaoh that the doubling of his dream meant “the matter is determined by God, and God will quickly bring it about” (Genesis 41:32). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

**Puns in the words.** Both the Pulpit Commentary and Constable note wordplays: *TEKEL* (weigh) plays on *qelal* (to be light/deficient), and *PERES* (divided) plays on *Paras* (Persia). The message carries a triple meaning in the last word: divided, half-shekel, and Persia. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-5.html]

**Clarke’s summary** (cited by Guzik): “MENE signifies NUMERATION; TEKEL, WEIGHING; and PERES, DIVISION.” God had Belshazzar’s number (it fell short), weighed him (he came up light), and would divide his kingdom. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

### v. 29 — “Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple…”

Belshazzar keeps his promise despite the devastating message. Guzik offers two possibilities: either Belshazzar believed Daniel and “bravely tried to do the best under the inevitable circumstances,” or he disbelieved and promoted Daniel “in a display of big-hearted fun.” Either way, Daniel’s promotion lasted only hours. Guzik remarks: “This shows how temporary the awards and accolades of this world are.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

Constable suggests another possibility: Belshazzar may have been drunk, or he may have repented — though any repentance was too late to avert judgment. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

### vv. 30–31 — “That very night Belshazzar… was slain, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom…”

**The fall of Babylon.** The Greek historian Herodotus (cited by Guzik and Constable) records that Cyrus’s engineers diverted the Euphrates River into a nearby swamp, lowering the water level so troops could march under the river-gates into the city. The bronze inner gates were left inexplicably unlocked. The city fell on the sixteenth of Tishri (October 11/12), 539 B.C., exactly as Isaiah (Isaiah 44:28–45:7) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 51:57–58) had prophesied over a century earlier. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]; [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]

Guzik notes the parallel: “The fall of mystery Babylon will be like the fall of real Babylon — sudden, sure, and in the midst of her worst blasphemies.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

**“Darius the Mede.”** This figure presents a well-known historical puzzle. Constable discusses four possible identifications: (1) a throne name for Cyrus himself; (2) Gubaru (Gobryas), a governor under Cyrus; (3) Ugbaru, the Persian general who led the assault (though different cuneiform signs for GU and UG argue against this); or (4) Cambyses, Cyrus’s son. He notes “there is no established fact which contradicts a person by the name of Darius the Mede reigning over Babylon if Darius is an alternate name for a known ruler.” Guzik identifies him as “a sub-king under Cyrus… referred to in secular history as Gubaru.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-5.html]; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-5/]

## TRADITIONAL READINGS: WHAT PROTESTANT COMMENTATORS AGREE ON

Across the sources consulted (Gill/Baptist, Guzik/Pentecostal-charismatic, Constable/evangelical, Pulpit Commentary/older Protestant), there is broad agreement on the core message of Daniel 5:

1. **Belshazzar’s feast was an act of deliberate sacrilege and pride**, not mere carelessness. He knew of Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling and defied Yahweh anyway.
2. **The handwriting was a direct, miraculous act of God**, not a psychological phenomenon.
3. **The wise men’s failure was divinely ordained** so that God’s man (Daniel) would be called.
4. **The three words are weight-names turned into judgment terms** through Daniel’s inspired interpretation: numbered, weighed, divided.
5. **The fall of Babylon that same night is historical fact** confirmed by multiple ancient sources (Herodotus, Xenophon, Berossus, the Nabonidus Chronicle, the Cyrus Cylinder).
6. **The chapter teaches that God rules over human kingdoms** and judges pride and blasphemy.

## AREAS WHERE PROTESTANT TRADITIONS MAY DIFFER

Because my search and fetch limits were reached, I was unable to retrieve full commentary from specific denominational sites (ligonier.org/Reformed, desiringgod.org/Baptist, seedbed.com/Methodist, lcms.org/Lutheran, etc.). The sources I did read (Gill, Guzik, Constable, Pulpit) do not highlight any major verse-level disagreements among Protestant traditions on this chapter. Possible areas where traditions might differ — but which I could not verify from those sites — include:

- **The exact identity of Darius the Mede**, where views vary among conservative commentators generally rather than along strict denominational lines.
- **Typological interpretations**: Some Reformed and Baptist commentators read Belshazzar’s feast as a type of the end-times “fall of Babylon” in Revelation 17–18 (this is noted by Guzik and Constable); some dispensational traditions place more weight on this typology than covenant theologians might.
